title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E420, Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 16, 1771/72). Euler's 'new and easy method' turns a variation into an ordinary partial derivative. The unknown z(x,y) is embedded in a one-parameter family z(x,y,t). The variation of a functional is then dt·∂/∂t of it. For a double integral ∬V dx dy, with V depending on z and its partial derivatives up to third order, §26 (previous page) wrote δ∬V dx dy as the sum of terms ∬N z_t, ∬P z_{xt}, ∬Q z_{xxt}, ∬R z_{xxxt}, ∬P' z_{yt}, ∬Q' z_{xyt}, and so on, each with measure dx dy. Here N = ∂V/∂z, P = ∂V/∂z_x, P' = ∂V/∂z_y, and so on.

On this page (§27–28) Euler removes the derivatives from z_t by integrating by parts one variable at a time.

(i) Second term, x varying only: ∫P z_{xt} dx = P z_t − ∫z_t P_x dx. Integrating over y gives ∬P z_{xt} dx dy = ∫P z_t dy − ∬z_t P_x dx dy.

(ii) Third term, y varying only: ∬P' z_{yt} dx dy = ∫P' z_t dx − ∬z_t P'_y dx dy.

(iii) Fourth term. Apply (i) with z_t replaced by z_{xt}: ∬Q z_{xxt} = ∫Q z_{xt} dy − ∬z_{xt} Q_x. Then apply (i) again with P replaced by Q_x: ∬z_{xt}Q_x = ∫z_t Q_x dy − ∬z_t Q_xx. The result is ∬Q z_{xxt} dx dy = ∫Q z_{xt} dy − ∫z_t Q_x dy + ∬z_t Q_xx dx dy.

The next page continues the same pattern for the mixed and third-order terms. Collecting the double-integral parts yields the coefficient of z_t:
N − P_x − P'_y + Q_xx + Q'_xy + Q''_yy − R_xxx − …
This is the Euler–Lagrange (Euler–Poisson/Ostrogradsky) equation for a double integral with higher derivatives. The single integrals are the boundary terms.
errors: §28, first formula: the left side reads ∬Q(d³z/dx²dt)dx; the factor dy is missing (a printing slip; it should be dx dy).

The boundary terms are written as indefinite single integrals, e.g. ∫P z_t dy with P z_t understood as evaluated at the x-limits. The domain is implicitly a rectangle (or a region with limits independent of the other variable). Euler does not treat curved boundaries, where the boundary terms must be combined into a line integral. This is a gap rather than an error, and it was resolved only later (Gauss, Poisson, Ostrogradsky, Sarrus).
Next page, not this one: 'loco P''' should read P'; and the section number 28 is repeated.

ideas.what: Iterated one-variable integration by parts to strip derivatives from the variation z_t in a double integral, including higher and mixed derivatives, separating interior (Euler–Lagrange) and boundary terms
ideas.modern_name: Integration by parts / Green–Gauss reduction yielding the Euler–Ostrogradsky equation with boundary terms
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–61) for double integrals; Euler E420 (1772); general multi-dimensional form Ostrogradsky (1834), Poisson (1833)
ideas.where_published: E420 itself; related material in Euler's variational papers E385/E386 (1771) and Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 3 appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Representing the variation as a partial derivative with respect to an auxiliary parameter t (z = z(x,y,t))
ideas.modern_name: First variation as d/dε of a one-parameter family (Gateaux derivative)
ideas.where_published: E420 and the Opera omnia I.25 editorial introduction (Carathéodory)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational page. The integrations by parts for double integrals in E420 are well documented in histories of the calculus of variations (Goldstine, Fraser, Carathéodory's Opera omnia introduction). The only notable points are a printing slip and the implicit restriction to a rectangular domain.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the missing dy in the §28 first formula; this is an error in the original print, not a transcription error.
In the third-term formula the original prints (ddz/dy.dt) with a stray period; this is harmless.
